meaning: A copy of a policy's weights saved during training; evaluation decides which checkpoint to keep.
The training objective computed on held-out demonstrations; for a diffusion policy, the error in predicting the added noise. It is open-loop.
The policy run as on the arm on each held-out frame, its action compared with the recorded one, usually as an MSE; meaningful only at a fixed number of denoising steps.
Scoring a policy on recorded frames by comparing the action it predicts with the recorded action; the policy's own actions never change what it sees next.
Letting the policy drive, on the bench, in a simulator or in a world model, so that each of its actions decides what it sees next, and counting successes.
The average squared distance between the policy's predicted action and the recorded action over the frames of a recording.
One complete run of a policy from the starting pose until the task succeeds, fails or runs out of time; also called a trial or an episode.
The number of rollouts that ended with the task done, divided by the number of rollouts.
A number between -1 and 1 that says how closely two lists of numbers rise and fall together; 1 means one predicts the other exactly, 0 means no relation.
The Pearson calculation applied to rank positions; it measures whether two ways of scoring put a set of policies in the same order.
The range of true success rates that could plausibly have produced the count that was observed; at the 95% level it contains the true rate about nineteen times in twenty.
A recipe for a confidence interval on a success rate that pulls the centre toward one half and keeps the width open at 0% and 100%; LeRobot's evaluation tool reports it.
The textbook interval p plus or minus z times sqrt(p(1-p)/n); it can run past 100% and collapses to zero width at a perfect score.
A test of whether two success counts could come from the same true rate: it counts how often luck alone would split the pooled failures at least as unevenly as observed.
How often two equally good policies would show a gap at least as large as the one observed.
The chance that a comparison detects a gap that is really there; 80% power detects it four times in five.
The false-alarm rate a comparison accepts when there is no gap; the 5% level is one time in twenty.

A comparison checked after each pair of trials that stops as soon as the evidence suffices, built so that the repeated checks do not raise the false-alarm rate; STEP (2025) proposes one for robot policies.
A fixed set of simulated tasks that everyone scores on, so results can be compared.
The state of a benchmark on which nearly every policy scores near the top, so the score no longer separates good policies from poor ones.
A suite of simulated manipulation tasks used as a benchmark, now saturated; LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-PRO are successors that perturb the scene.
LeRobot's evaluation tool: it runs a checkpoint closed loop in a batch of simulated environments and reports the success rate with a 95% Wilson interval.
NVIDIA's evaluation tool for its Isaac Lab simulator, with perturbation sweeps over lighting, backgrounds, camera parameters and object mass.
Scoring the same checkpoint across controlled changes to one scene (lighting, backgrounds, camera parameters, object mass) and keeping only checkpoints whose rate holds.
Closed-loop scoring in which a video world model generates what the cameras would show after each action and a vision-language model judges the generated video.
A model that takes images and text as input; used here as the judge of a generated rollout.
A real-robot ranking of policies built from blind pairwise comparisons run at seven academic institutions on the DROID platform; the reference that simulators and world models are compared with.
The robot platform RoboArena's evaluators share, so that every lab runs policies on the same model of robot.

expansion: International Conference on Robotics and Automation
meaning: A robotics research conference; the REAL-I robot challenge held there in 2026 published a report cited for what open-loop error misses.
A robot challenge held at ICRA 2026; its report names the closed-loop effects open-loop error misses, and one of its teams used open-loop prediction to shortlist checkpoints.
The difference between how a policy does in the simulator and on the real arm; more simulated trials do not shrink it (section 14).
A simulated environment that steps physics and hands the policy joint and object states, with no simulated camera; the cheapest kind to run.
